Introduction
When I first started learning Python, I thought variables stored values directly. For example, I believed that when I wrote x = 5, the number 5 was simply stored inside the variable x. However, as I learned more about Python, I discovered that Python works in a different way. In Python, everything is an object, and variables do not store values directly. Instead, they store references to objects created in memory.
Understanding how Python handles objects, memory, mutability, and function arguments is very important because it helps developers avoid unexpected behaviors and write better programs. In this article, I will explain these concepts using simple examples and memory diagrams to make them easier to understand.
Understanding Objects in Python
In Python, everything we use is an object. Numbers, strings, lists, functions, and even classes are objects. Every object has three important characteristics:

• A value

• A type

• An identity
The value represents the information stored inside the object. The type tells Python what kind of object it is, and the identity is a unique identifier that allows Python to recognize that object during its lifetime.
For example:
x = 10
print(type(x))
print(id(x))
Output:
<class ‘int’>
140218463129232
The type() function tells us the class of the object. In this example, x is an integer object.
The id() function returns a unique identifier for the object. In CPython, this identifier is usually related to the object’s location in memory.
A simple representation:
Variable
x
│
▼
+ — — — +
| 10 |
+ — — — +
type → int
id → unique identifier
Object Identity and References
Since variables store references to objects, two variables can point to the same object.
Example:
x = 10
y = x
print(id(x))
print(id(y))
Both variables have the same identity because they reference the same object.
Memory representation:
x ─┐
│
▼
+ — — — +
| 10 |
+ — — — +
▲
│
y ─┘
Python also provides two ways to compare objects:
print(x == y)
print(x is y)
The difference is:

• == compares the values of two objects.

• is compares whether two variables refer to the exact same object.
For example, two different lists can have the same values but not be the same object.
Mutable Objects
A mutable object is an object that can be changed after it is created without changing its identity.
Some examples of mutable objects in Python are:

• Lists

• Dictionaries

• Sets

• Bytearrays
For example:
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
print(id(numbers))
numbers.append(4)
print(id(numbers))
The content of the list changes, but the identity remains the same.
Before:
numbers
↓
[1,2,3]
After:
numbers
↓
[1,2,3,4]
Python modified the existing object instead of creating a new one.
Another example with a dictionary:
student = {
“name”: “Alice”
}
student[“age”] = 18
print(student)
Output:
{‘name’: ‘Alice’, ‘age’: 18}
The dictionary was modified directly because dictionaries are mutable objects.
Immutable Objects
Immutable objects are objects that cannot be modified after they are created. If we try to change them, Python creates a new object instead.
Examples of immutable objects include:

• Integers

• Floats

• Complex numbers

• Booleans

• Strings

• Tuples

• Frozen sets

• Bytes
Example:
name = “John”
print(id(name))
name += “ Smith”
print(id(name))
The original string is not changed. Python creates a new string object.
Before:
name
↓
“John”
After:
name
↓
“John Smith”
The identity changes because a new object was created.
Assignment Does Not Copy Objects
One common mistake for beginners is thinking that assigning one variable to another creates a copy.
Example:
a = [1,2]
b = a
Many people think Python creates two different lists. However, Python only copies the reference.
Memory representation:
a ───┐
│
▼
[1,2]
▲
│
b ───┘
Both variables point to the same object.
Therefore:
b.append(3)
print(a)
Output:
[1,2,3]
Changing b also changes a because they are aliases.
An alias means that two variables refer to the same object.
Why Does Mutability Matter?
Understanding mutable and immutable objects is important because it affects how programs behave.
Mutable objects can create unexpected results when different variables share the same object. A change made through one variable can affect another variable.
Immutable objects are safer in many situations because they cannot be changed after creation.
This is also why immutable objects like strings, numbers, and tuples can be used as dictionary keys.
Passing Arguments to Functions in Python
Python uses a system called pass-by-assignment when passing arguments to functions.
This means that functions receive a reference to the same object.
For mutable objects:
def add_item(lst):
lst.append(4)
numbers = [1,2,3]
add_item(numbers)
print(numbers)
Output:
[1,2,3,4]
The function modified the original list because the list is mutable.
Memory representation:
numbers
↓
[1,2,3]
↓
Function
↓
lst
↓
Same object
However, immutable objects behave differently.
Example:
def increment(x):
x += 1
a = 5
increment(a)
print(a)
Output:
5
The value of a does not change because integers are immutable. Python creates a new integer object instead of modifying the original one.
Integer Pre-allocation in Python
Python has an optimization called integer pre-allocation.
In CPython, small integers are created when Python starts and reused throughout the program. This helps improve performance because small numbers are used very often.
The range is usually:
-5 to 256
These values are stored and reused.
For example:
a = 100
b = 100
print(a is b)
The result may be:
True
because both variables may point to the same pre-created integer object.
However, programmers should not use is to compare numbers. The correct way is always:
a == b
The constants used internally by CPython include:

• NSMALLPOSINTS = 257

• NSMALLNEGINTS = 5
These allow Python to manage commonly used integers efficiently.
The Special Case of Tuples and Frozen Sets
Tuples and frozen sets are immutable objects, but they can contain mutable objects.
Example:
t = ([1,2],3)
t[0].append(5)
print(t)
Output:
([1,2,5],3)
The tuple itself did not change. The list inside the tuple changed because lists are mutable.
However:
t[0] = [9]
will produce:
TypeError
because replacing an element inside a tuple is not allowed.
The same idea applies to frozen sets. A frozenset is the immutable version of a set.
Conclusion
When I started learning Python, the idea that everything is an object was confusing. I used to think variables directly stored values, but I learned that variables actually store references to objects in memory.
Understanding concepts such as id(), type(), mutable objects, immutable objects, aliasing, and pass-by-assignment helped me understand why Python behaves the way it does.
These concepts are important for every Python programmer because they help prevent common mistakes and make code easier to understand. After learning about Python’s object model, I now have a clearer view of how Python manages data behind the scenes.
